paras: The Evansville mob assault on John Hawkins took place on the evening of July 28, 1903, when a mob chased and assaulted Hawkins, a Black man, on the streets of Evansville, Indiana. The next morning a city judge fined one participant, Jacob Keil, and two other young men were arrested as members of the mob, one of whom, Albert Merkel, was later tried for assault and battery. Papers noted the case for the judge's declaration that Black people had the same rights as whites under the law, and as one of a series of 'race outbreaks' in the city after rioting earlier that month.

Evansville had seen rioting in early July 1903 after Robert Lee, described as a Black man, shot and killed police officer Louis Massey on July 3. On the evening of July 6 a clash between a mob and the local company of state militia left ten people dead, according to a coroner's verdict returned on August 1 that did not fix blame. Tension had not ended by late July: the Evansville correspondent called the attack on Hawkins 'the second' outbreak since the Danville riot and lynching of the preceding Sunday, and three youths later pleaded guilty to stoning the houses of Black residents on the night of Monday, July 27.

On the evening of Tuesday, July 28, a mob pursued Hawkins through the streets and assaulted him. The July 29 dispatch said he 'came near faring badly at the hands of a mob', and a later report described him as assaulted 'by a gang' and said he 'had a narrow escape'. Neither report gives a cause for the chase, names an accusation against Hawkins, or describes any injury to him.

On the morning of July 29 Judge Mattison fined Jacob Keil, eighteen, $10 and costs for his part in chasing and assaulting Hawkins, and Keil was sent to jail, in default of payment according to the Indianapolis Journal's headline. Albert Merkel and George Walters were under arrest, charged with being members of the mob, and the dispatch said others would be taken into custody. Both the court and the prosecutor said that Hawkins would have been legally justified had he turned and fired on his pursuers, although the dispatch added that 'the probabilities are that a lynching would have followed.'

Mattison declared from the bench that Black people had 'the same rights as white people under the law' and warned that unless 'these race outbreaks' ceased he would deal 'most vigorously' with offenders. By August 1 Merkel, nineteen, had been tried in the city court for assault and battery on Hawkins, and the judge postponed his decision. No report of a verdict in Merkel's case, of the disposition of Walters's case, or of further arrests appears in the coverage.

The case reached print through Evansville correspondents' reports of the city court, published on July 30 in the Indianapolis Journal and the Louisville Courier-Journal in nearly identical form. The Journal headlined its item 'FINE FOR NEGRO BAITER', with subheads stressing the jail sentence and the pursuit of 'a Negro Through the Streets', and built the story around the court's response rather than any grievance of the attackers. The Courier-Journal ran the same facts as an Evansville special on page 8 among unrelated Indiana and Louisville news, with small differences of wording, such as the judge saying that whites had 'no reason' rather than 'no right' to persecute Black people.

The Journal's follow-up on August 2 reduced the case to a few lines at the end of a story on the coroner's verdict on the July riot deaths. Both papers set the assault beside news of the earlier rioting, including a report that Robert Lee's wife, who had fled the city on the night of the riot, had been killed on a railroad bridge near Madisonville, Kentucky. All coverage of the Hawkins case found is in white papers; no Black-press report of it was found.

bases: A mob chased and assaulted one Black man on the street, with no killing reported, and participants were fined or charged with assault (A2, A3, A4).

The July 29 Evansville dispatch (A2, A3, near-identical texts likely from one Evansville source) and a separate Aug. 1 dispatch reporting Merkel's trial (A4) agree that Hawkins was chased and assaulted by a mob or gang, though all come from Evansville correspondents' court reporting.

accounts.label: Evansville dispatch of July 29 (court report)
accounts.gist: Hawkins was chased and assaulted by a mob the previous evening and nearly 'fared badly'; Keil was fined and jailed and two others arrested, and the judge said whites had no right to persecute negroes.

accounts.label: Evansville dispatch of Aug. 1 (court report)
accounts.gist: Hawkins had been assaulted by a gang 'last Tuesday' and had a narrow escape; Merkel was tried for assault and battery and the decision postponed.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal headlined the item 'FINE FOR NEGRO BAITER' and led with the punishment and the judge's statement that whites had no right to persecute negroes.
The Courier-Journal ran the Evansville special without comment among Indiana and Louisville items on page 8.
The Journal's follow-up placed Merkel's trial in the last lines of a story on the coroner's verdict on the July riot deaths.
